(Nasdaq: KMTS), a leading wearable medical device and digital healthcare company, today announced publication of primary results from the ASSURE® WCD Clinical Evaluation Post-Approval Study (ACE-PAS) in the Journal of Cardiovascular Electrophysiology. The largest prospective real-world study of wearable cardioverter defibrillators (WCD) to date, ACE-PAS enrolled 21,612 patients across 35 U.S. states and met both primary safety and effectiveness endpoints. The study demonstrated 100% all-shock conversion success and sustained daily wear, while documenting ventricular arrhythmias early and continuously over subsequent months. The findings strengthen the clinical case for the ASSURE system across WCD indications and underscore the importance of protecting patients throughout periods of elevated arrhythmic risk.

headlines.title: From AI to oil, here are Goldman and Morgan Stanley’s outlooks for 2027
headlines.summary: Global growth is going to continue, albeit at different forecasts, according to Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs.
headlines.article_text: What Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley expect for markets in 2027 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Global growth is going to continue, albeit at different forecasts, according to Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs. Both firms say the growth will be partly powered by robust AI spending, but differ on how inflation, energy prices and interest rates will shape the year ahead. Morgan Stanley recommends a “maximum overweight” position in global equities, favoring the U.S., Japan and Europe. As 2026 draws to a close, investors are asking a simple question: What will 2027 bring? The passing year saw massive upheavals and market swings, including the Iran War, volatile oil prices, a reckoning in the AI industry — of course, including the Nvidia shakeup — and a U.S. midterm election that shifted control of Congress to Democrats. In their 2027 outlooks, Wall Street giants Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley share a broad conclusion: Global economic growth should continue, though they diverge on the pace. Goldman expects global growth of 2.8% next year, up from 2.7% in 2026 in its Macro Outlook 2027 report, while Morgan Stanley’s baseline forecast puts growth at 3.4%, down from 3.5% this year, according to its 2027 Global Strategy Outlook. Both banks expect robust AI spending to remain a source of growth, but they differ on how inflation, energy prices and interest rates could shape the year ahead — differences that could lead investors toward markedly varied strategies. AI growth with oil risks Goldman expects lower energy prices and continued artificial intelligence investment to support global growth in 2027, offsetting tighter financial conditions and a less supportive fiscal backdrop. The bank expects Brent crude to ease to $78 a barrel by the end of next year, while Morgan Stanley forecasts Brent at $75 a barrel in the fourth quarter of 2027. Morgan Stanley, however, sees energy costs remaining high enough in the near term to weigh on economic activity and keep inflation elevated, according to its 2027 Global Economics Outlook report. The firms also differ on inflation and monetary policy. Goldman sees the Federal Reserve returning to rate cuts late in 2027, while Morgan Stanley expects cuts to resume in 2028. AI investment remains a key source of support in both forecasts, though the firms emphasize different risks. Goldman expects spending on AI to keep rising, though its contribution to growth may moderate. Morgan Stanley says its baseline AI investment forecasts remain intact, but warns that weaker-than-expected spending could weigh on growth both directly and through lower asset prices. In Asian economies heavily exposed to the AI boom, including South Korea and Taiwan, Goldman expects AI-related exports to continue supporting growth, though the pace will moderate, according to its Asia 2027 Outlook report. Morgan Stanley similarly sees growth in North Asia slowing down as the rapid expansion in technology exports normalizes. In China, it expects export strength to help cushion weak domestic demand and the ongoing property downturn. Stock market ratings Both banks expect equities to rise in 2027, though Morgan Stanley is more bullish, recommending a "maximum overweight" position in global stocks and favoring the U.S., Japan and Europe. It forecasts 13% earnings growth for the MSCI All Country World Index in 2027. Morgan Stanley gives an "equal weight" rating on emerging markets, but in Asia, it favors Japan, Korea, Singapore and Thailand, and is neutral on Taiwan, China and India. It expects 2026 market leaders such as Japan, South Korea and Taiwan’s technology sector to continue outperforming, rather than a broad rotation into markets that lagged this year like Australia, China and India. That view reflects a more cautious earnings outlook for emerging markets. Morgan Stanley forecasts 17% earnings growth in 2027, below the 29% consensus estimate, largely because of its more cautious stance on China. Goldman Sachs also expects the global equity bull market to continue, supported by earnings growth and the prospect of lower inflation, oil prices and bond yields, said analysts led by Peter Oppenheimer and Sharon Bell. The bank is "overweight" U.S. and Japanese equities, but more cautious elsewhere compared to Morgan Stanley, with neutral calls on Asia and emerging markets, as well as advising investors to underweight Europe. Goldman also warned that market returns will become increasingly sensitive to whether AI spending continues to translate into earnings growth. Dollar divide While both firms are broadly aligned on the growth outlook, they diverge more sharply on currencies — particularly the dollar. In its 2027 Global FX Outlook report, Goldman expects the dollar’s mixed performance in 2026 to give way to a softer path over 2027. Its Asia strategists, led by Danny Suwanapruti and Chris Poh, see lower oil prices, continued AI investment and a more dovish Federal Reserve path than markets currently expect as supportive for Asian currencies. "Our economic forecasts lead us to expect that the Fed and European Central Bank will hike rates in December and the Fed again in March before both return to rate cuts in late 2027," Goldman said. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley expects "modest" dollar strength, citing interest-rate differentials between the U.S. and other economies. It sees Asian currencies weakening broadly as elevated U.S. yields and low regional carry weigh on the region. One exception is the Chinese yuan. "Resilient exports, continued exporter FX conversion and tighter management of capital outflows keep U.S. dollar/Chinese RMB broadly stable despite soft domestic demand," Morgan Stanley said. Some Southeast Asian currencies could also remain relatively resilient, such as the Malaysian ringgit and Singapore dollar as potential regional outperformers. Bonds and credit In bond markets, Goldman expects two more rate hikes from the Fed and one from the European Central Bank before both return to rate cuts in late 2027. The bank said most of its forecasts for other central banks are also below current market pricing, leading it to expect longer-term yields to decline. That drop, however, could be partly offset by large government deficits and heavy AI-related borrowing. Morgan Stanley, meanwhile, sees AI as a key driver of the credit-market story in 2027, much as it has been this year. "Our U.S. corporate credit strategists see $2.4 trillion of U.S. investment grade gross issuance next year, translating to about $1.1 trillion of net debt added to the market, in large part to satisfy hyperscaler funding needs," the bank said. Morgan Stanley also favors higher-quality corporate credit over lower-rated debt, arguing that elevated interest rates leave riskier borrowers more exposed. In Asia, the bank expects the rates outlook to become more constructive as central banks approach the end of their tightening cycles, with some easing later in 2027.
